cards.q: What is a gravitational field?
cards.a: A region in which a mass experiences a force, without contact.

cards.q: Define gravitational field strength at a point.
cards.a: The force per unit mass on a small mass placed at that point: \(g = \frac{F}{m}\). Unit: \(\text{N kg}^{-1}\).

cards.q: State Newton's law of gravitation.
cards.a: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: \(F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\). It is always attractive.

cards.q: State the unit of the gravitational constant \(G\).

Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth (mass \(5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\), radius \(6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\)) and a 70 kg person on its surface. (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}\))
cards.a: 690 N
steps: The separation is the distance between centres: the Earth's radius.
cards.why: This is the person's weight: the same as \(mg\).

cards.q: A satellite orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface. A student uses \(r = 400\ \text{km}\) in \(F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\). What is wrong?
cards.a: \(r\) is the distance between the centres of the two masses. It should be the Earth's radius plus the height: \(6.37 \times 10^{6} + 0.40 \times 10^{6} = 6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\).

cards.q: Derive the expression for the gravitational field strength at a distance \(r\) from a point mass \(M\).
steps: The force on a small mass \(m\) at distance \(r\) is \(F = \frac{GMm}{r^{2}}\).
Field strength is force per unit mass: \(g = \frac{F}{m}\).

cards.q: Calculate the gravitational field strength 400 km above the Earth's surface. (\(GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\) for the Earth; radius \(6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\))
cards.a: \(8.7\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Still about 90% of its surface value: astronauts in orbit are not beyond gravity.

cards.q: The distance from the centre of a planet doubles. How does the gravitational field strength change?
cards.a: It falls to one quarter: field strength follows an inverse-square law.
cards.why: Writing only that it "decreases with distance" does not earn the mark: say inverse-square.

cards.q: Describe the gravitational field lines around a planet, and close to its surface.
cards.a: Around the planet: radial, pointing towards its centre, and further apart at greater distances. Close to the surface: parallel and equally spaced, showing a uniform field.

cards.q: Define gravitational potential at a point.
cards.a: The work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point. Unit: \(\text{J kg}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Why is gravitational potential always negative?
cards.a: Potential is defined as zero at infinity. Gravity is attractive, so work must be done on a mass to move it out to infinity: everywhere closer has less potential than zero.

cards.q: Write the equation for the gravitational potential at a distance \(r\) from a point mass \(M\).
cards.a: \(V = -\frac{GM}{r}\)

cards.q: Calculate the gravitational potential at the Earth's surface. (\(GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\); radius \(6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\))
cards.a: \(-6.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Keep the minus sign in the answer.

cards.q: A 400 kg satellite is moved from a point where the gravitational potential is \(-6.25 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\) to one where it is \(-5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\). Calculate the work done.
cards.a: \(5.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: What is an equipotential surface, and how much work is done moving a mass along one?
cards.a: A surface on which the potential is the same everywhere. No work is done moving a mass along it.
cards.why: Equipotentials are always at right angles to field lines.

cards.q: How is the gravitational field strength found from a graph of potential \(V\) against distance \(r\)?
cards.a: It is minus the gradient: \(g = -\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}\).

cards.q: What does the area under a graph of gravitational field strength \(g\) against distance \(r\) represent?
cards.a: The change in gravitational potential between the two distances.

cards.q: Describe how \(g\) and \(V\) vary with distance \(r\) from the centre of a planet, outside the planet.
cards.a: \(g\) falls as \(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\): a steep curve that approaches zero. \(V\) is negative and rises towards zero as \(-\frac{1}{r}\): a shallower curve.

cards.q: Derive an expression for the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) around a planet of mass \(M\).
cards.a: \(v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}\)
cards.why: The satellite's own mass cancels: every satellite at that radius has the same speed.

cards.q: Show that, for a satellite in a circular orbit, \(T^{2} \propto r^{3}\).
steps: Gravity provides the centripetal force: \(\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = m\omega^{2}r\).
\(\frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}\) is constant for a given planet, so \(T^{2} \propto r^{3}\).

cards.q: Calculate the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(6.77 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\) around the Earth. (\(GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(7.7 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

cards.q: Calculate the radius of a geostationary orbit around the Earth. (\(GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\); period 24 hours)
cards.a: \(4.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}\)
cards.why: This is measured from the centre of the Earth: about 36 000 km above the surface.

cards.q: State three features of a geostationary orbit.
cards.a: Its period is 24 hours, it is in the plane of the equator, and the satellite moves in the same direction as the Earth's rotation. It therefore stays above the same point on the Earth.

cards.q: Give one use of a geostationary satellite and one use of a satellite in low orbit.
cards.a: Geostationary: communications and television, because a fixed dish can point at it. Low orbit: imaging, weather and surveillance, because it is close to the surface and passes over all of it as the Earth turns beneath.

cards.q: Derive the expression for the escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass \(M\) and radius \(r\).
cards.a: \(v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}\)
steps: To escape, the object must reach infinity, where its potential energy is zero.
Its kinetic energy at the surface must at least equal the gain in potential energy: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{GMm}{r}\).
cards.why: The escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the object.

cards.q: Calculate the escape velocity from the Earth's surface. (\(GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\); radius \(6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\))
cards.a: \(1.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

cards.q: For a satellite of mass \(m\) in a circular orbit of radius \(r\), write its kinetic energy, its potential energy and its total energy.
cards.a: Kinetic: \(\frac{GMm}{2r}\). Potential: \(-\frac{GMm}{r}\). Total: \(-\frac{GMm}{2r}\).
cards.why: The total is negative: the satellite is bound to the planet.

cards.q: A satellite moves to a circular orbit of smaller radius. What happens to its speed, its potential energy and its total energy?
cards.a: Its speed increases, its potential energy decreases (becomes more negative), and its total energy decreases.
cards.why: It gains kinetic energy, but loses twice as much potential energy.

cards.q: Why do astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless, although gravity still acts on them?
cards.a: The astronauts and the spacecraft are both in free fall, with the same acceleration towards the Earth. So the spacecraft exerts no contact force on them, and it is the contact force that gives the sensation of weight.

cards.q: Give two similarities and one difference between gravitational fields and electric fields.
cards.a: Similarities: both obey an inverse-square law for the force between point objects, and both can be described by field lines and by potential. Difference: gravity is always attractive, but electric forces can attract or repel.
